Deal-level intelligence · v0.1

Who gets to own Quebec infrastructure.

Quebec is building the largest energy expansion in its history and its mid-market is changing hands. Most of the record sits in French — Régie de l'énergie dockets, Hydro-Québec tender results, provincial decrees — and is read by almost no one on Bay Street or in New York.

This tracker reads those filings and publishes them as structured English. Every figure carries its source and a confidence flag R-4227-2023. Where a number is sealed, it says so instead of estimating.

Pipeline, not yet financed

Quebec announces capacity years before it reaches financial close. That gap is public, it is written in French, and it is where the next decade of project finance mandates comes from.

04

Method

What gets recorded

Sponsor and sponsor type, asset and asset type, capacity, province, stage, offtake counterparty and tenor, rating, acquirer origin and capital source. Each field carries its own source and date, not one citation for the whole row.

The disclosure cliff

Privatization is itself a disclosure event. When a Quebec issuer goes private, its filings stop and its press archive is often pruned — Innergex now retains five press items and no investor section. Boralex will follow at close. This tracker records the last public state of an asset before the record closes, because after that no amount of searching recovers it.

What does not

Per-developer PPA pricing, debt tranche margins, mezzanine terms and mid-market multiples are sealed or redacted in Quebec filings. They are marked confidential rather than estimated. A tracker that guesses at them is worth less than one that admits the boundary.

Confidence flags

Disclosed stated by a party or a regulator. Reported from credible secondary press, not yet confirmed in a filing. Confidential exists but is sealed. Unverified carried from secondary reporting and not yet confirmed in a primary document — shown so the gap is visible rather than hidden.

Primary sources

  • Régie de l'énergie dockets, decisions
  • Hydro-Québec appels d'offres, Plan 2035
  • DBRS Morningstar rating reports
  • SEDAR+ issuer filings
  • Canada Infrastructure Bank participations
  • BAPE hearings, decrees
05

Notes

Short pieces published when the data says something the consensus does not.

No. 3 · August 2026

Quebec is funding 2035 with forty-year paper, and the whole street is in the book.

On 7 August, Hydro-Québec reopened its Series JU bonds for another C$500M — a 4.00% coupon priced at 84.479 to yield 4.900%, maturing in February 2065. It was the seventeenth reopening of a line first issued in September 2024. That series alone now stands at C$9.0B.

The syndicate is the tell. RBC led, with National Bank and TD as co-leads, and BMO, CIBC, Scotia, Desjardins, Laurentian and Casgrain filling out the book. Every major Canadian dealer is underwriting the buildout, which is what you would expect when a single provincial utility is carrying a 10,000 MW wind target and the transmission to move it.

It also frames where the private opportunity is not. Hydro-Québec funds itself at forty-year tenors in the public market at prices no project sponsor can match. Private capital does not compete with that. It shows up further down the structure — in the developer equity, the partnership stakes, and the project debt behind tenders like A/O 2026-01, where bids close in February.

No. 2 · August 2026

The A25 is what the wall looks like in slow motion.

Transurban, an Australian toll-road operator, sold half of the A25 concession to La Caisse in 2023. In June 2026 it sold the rest, for C$280M in equity. Operations move to Plenary Americas, itself a La Caisse portfolio company. A foreign infrastructure investor is now fully out of one of only two public-private tolled highways in Quebec, and the provincial fund owns all of it and runs it through its own operator.

Boralex shows the same move with the steps visible. La Caisse has been a shareholder and a lender there since 2017. In July 2025 it and Fondaction put C$250M of subordinated debt into the company. Eight months later it agreed to take it private alongside Brookfield, rolling from roughly 15% to 30%. Lender, then shareholder, then owner.

Read alongside Innergex, the sequence stops looking like unrelated deals. Foreign and out-of-province capital is not being blocked at the door — it is being bought out, in stages, on friendly terms, by an institution with a longer horizon and a mandate that is not purely financial.

For a lender or a sponsor looking at Quebec infrastructure, the practical question is not whether you can get in. It is what your exit looks like, and who the buyer will be when you want one.

No. 1 · August 2026

Quebec's mid-market is not being bought. It is being walled.

The convenient story is that outside capital is pouring into Quebec. The transactions do not support it. CDPQ took Innergex private outright. Fengate's eStruxture recapitalization cashed out a Quebec institution rather than displacing one. And Boralex is the cleanest case of all: Brookfield did not buy it around La Caisse, it bought it with La Caisse, which rolled its roughly 15% stake up to 30% of the private company. The head office stays in Quebec.

Where out-of-province buyers did win control, they did it in two lanes: take-privates of listed companies, where a public bid cannot be quietly pre-empted, and digital infrastructure, where the domestic bench is thinner and the capital requirement is larger than a provincial balance sheet wants to carry alone.

The wall is not purely defensive, and the tracker should say so. Novacap closed a US$3.8B technology fund in February 2026 and is deploying it into Buffalo, Nashville, Tampa, Idaho and Kentucky. Quebec capital consolidates at home and buys abroad at the same time. The pattern is asymmetric, not closed.

The next test is A/O 2026-01. Bids close in February. Watch whether the winning consortia are domestic-led with foreign money behind them, and whether that changes the financing structures that follow.
